edges.rationale: Naming a note on the grand staff starts with counting which line or space it sits on.
Every note on the grand staff is named with one of the seven letters.
The grand staff's upper staff is read in the treble clef.
The grand staff's lower staff is read in the bass clef.
Middle C is the note that joins the grand staff's two staves.
Notes beyond either staff of the grand staff are written on ledger lines.
A note name on the grand staff is incomplete until any sharp, flat or natural is read with it.
Landmark notes are the grand-staff positions readers memorise first and count from.
The grand staff maps to the keyboard, and each named note becomes a key found from the black-key groups.
Octave signs change which octave a grand-staff note sounds in without changing where it is written.
Stems are drawn by a note's place on the staff, a side detail of grand-staff notation.
Rewriting between clefs tests that each clef's note names are known at the same pitch.
Reading the treble staff at the keyboard is grand-staff naming turned into keys.
Reading the bass staff at the keyboard is grand-staff naming turned into keys.
Lines that cross middle C use both staves of the grand staff at once.
The treble clef gives the five lines and four spaces their names.
The bass clef gives the five lines and four spaces their names.
A step is a line to the next space; a skip is a line to the next line.
Stem direction is decided by a note's position relative to the middle line.
Interval sizes are counted in letter names, both ends included.
The seven letters repeat at every octave.
The same staff position has different names in the two clefs, so a reader used to one misreads the other by two letters.
The alto clef's lines sit one letter above the treble clef's, a frequent source of misreadings.
Both are C clefs: the clef marks middle C on a line, the third for alto and the fourth for tenor.
The two C clefs sit one line apart, so their notes are easily confused.
Both clefs name one landmark line, G for treble and F for bass, and every other note is counted from it.
Transcription exercises at Grade 5 move melodies into and out of the alto clef.
Transcription exercises at Grade 5 move melodies into and out of the tenor clef.
The alto clef is defined by where it puts middle C.
The tenor clef is defined by where it puts middle C.
Middle C is the first ledger-line note most readers meet.
Middle C, C4, is where the octave numbering is anchored for most readers.
Middle C is the central landmark of the grand staff.
Treble G is the landmark the treble clef is drawn around.
Bass F is the landmark the bass clef is drawn around.
Readers name an unknown note by stepping or skipping from the nearest landmark.
Both handle notes beyond the staff; octave signs replace long stacks of ledger lines.
Moving a note into another clef often lands it on ledger lines.
Knowing what an accidental does is not enough without knowing how long it lasts.
Sharps and flats each move a note by one semitone.
Double sharps and double flats move a note by two semitones instead of one.
Sharps and flats give each black key two names.
The missing black keys between E-F and B-C are where white keys sit a semitone apart.
E sharp is F because E to F is already a semitone.
F double sharp is the key G: double accidentals are read through enharmonic spelling.
One key, many names: the habit of one letter per key breaks on E sharp, C flat and double accidentals.
The black-key groups repeat across the 88 keys, one set per octave.
Octave numbers name which copy of a letter is meant.
An octave sign moves notes to the same letters an octave away.
An accidental applies only to its own staff position, not to the same letter in other octaves.
Finding a named key is done from the black-key groups.
A key is found by its letter name.
Playing in a register means finding the octave number on the keyboard.
The same tune in another octave keeps its letters.
Reading treble notes at the keyboard uses the treble clef's names.
Each name read must land on its key.
Reading bass notes at the keyboard uses the bass clef's names.
Each name read must land on its key.
The same skill on the other staff: name, find, play.
Playing ledger notes means counting ledger lines in time.
Ledger notes extend treble reading above and below the staff.
Playing sharps and flats puts the accidental rules on the keys.
An accidental early in a bar must be played again on later notes without a sign.
E sharp, B sharp, C flat and F flat are played through their enharmonic white keys.
Double accidentals are played the same way, by finding the key the spelling means.
Unusual spellings are the hardest case of playing accidentals.
Playing under 8va or 8vb is the octave sign read in real time.
An octave sign is a forced change of register.
A position starts from finding its first key.
Inside a position, a step is the next finger and a skip skips one.
A shift moves the hand from one five-finger position to another.
Seeing a leap on the page warns the hand that a shift is coming.
Reading by intervals is seeing steps and skips and playing them.
Interval reading works on top of knowing a few notes by name.
Sight-reading keeps tempo by reading shapes rather than naming every note.
A single line at sight needs quick note reading in its clef.
A single line at sight needs quick note reading in its clef.
A line crosses between the staves at middle C.
The right hand's part of a crossing line is read in the treble staff.
The left hand's part of a crossing line is read in the bass staff.

items.prompt: How many lines and spaces does one staff have?

answer.explanation: A staff is five lines; the gaps between them make four spaces.

wrong.explanation: That counts the area above or below the staff as a space; only the four gaps between the lines are the staff's spaces.
Lines and spaces are swapped: there are five lines, and the four spaces sit between them.
A sixth line would be a ledger line added for one note, not part of the staff.

items.prompt: Which line of the staff is the first line?

answer.explanation: Lines and spaces are counted from the bottom up, so the first line is the lowest.

wrong.explanation: Counting runs upward, the same way pitch rises, so the top line is the fifth.
The middle line is the third line, two lines up from the bottom.
The clef names a line's pitch but does not change how lines are numbered: always bottom to top.

items.prompt: Going up from G, which letter name comes next?

answer.explanation: The musical alphabet runs A B C D E F G and then starts again at A.

wrong.explanation: English note names stop at G; there is no H in English usage.
F is below G; going up from G wraps around to A.
The next G is seven letters up; the very next step is A.

items.prompt: How many different letter names do notes use?

answer.explanation: A, B, C, D, E, F and G: after G the names repeat.

wrong.explanation: Eight counts the starting letter twice, as in C up to the next C; there are only seven names.
Twelve is the number of different keys in an octave, white and black; the black keys reuse the seven letters with sharps or flats.
Five is the number of black keys in an octave, not the number of letter names.

items.prompt: In the treble clef, which note is on the top line?

answer.explanation: Treble lines from the bottom are E G B D F, so the top line is F5.

wrong.explanation: E is the bottom line (E4) and the fourth space (E5); the top line is F.
G5 sits in the space just above the staff; the top line is one step lower, F5.
A4 is the second space (F A C E); it is not a line note.

items.prompt: In the treble clef, which note is in the third space?

answer.explanation: Treble spaces from the bottom spell F A C E, so the third space is C5.

wrong.explanation: A is the second space; counting starts at the bottom space, F.
B4 is the middle line, just below the third space.
E5 is the fourth (top) space.

items.prompt: In the bass clef, which note is on the bottom line?

answer.explanation: Bass lines from the bottom are G B D F A, so the bottom line is G2.

wrong.explanation: E is the treble clef's bottom line; read in bass clef the same line is G, two letters higher.
F3 is the fourth line, the one between the clef's two dots.
A2 is the bottom space; the bottom line is a step lower, G2.

items.prompt: Which line do the two dots of the bass clef surround?

answer.explanation: The bass clef is an F clef: its dots sit either side of the fourth line, F3.

wrong.explanation: The dots surround the fourth line from the bottom, not the second.
D3 is the middle line; the dots sit one line higher, around F.
The line is F3, below middle C; F4 is in the treble staff's bottom space.

items.prompt: Where is middle C written on the grand staff?

answer.text: On one ledger line, below the treble staff or above the bass staff
answer.explanation: C4 is one ledger line below the treble staff; the same pitch is one ledger line above the bass staff.

wrong.text: In the third space of the treble staff
wrong.explanation: The third treble space is C5, the C an octave above middle C.

wrong.text: In the second space of the bass staff
wrong.explanation: The second bass space is C3, the C an octave below middle C.

wrong.text: On the middle line of the treble staff
wrong.explanation: The treble middle line is B4, seven white keys above middle C.

items.prompt: In American Standard Pitch Notation, what is middle C called?

answer.explanation: ASPN numbers octaves from C; the C near the middle of the piano begins octave 4.

wrong.explanation: C3 is an octave lower, written in the bass staff's second space. (Some music software calls middle C 'C3', but standard notation uses C4.)
C1 is near the bottom of the piano, three octaves below middle C.
C5 is the C an octave above, in the treble staff's third space.

items.prompt: In the treble clef, which note sits on the first ledger line above the staff?

answer.explanation: The top line is F5, the space above is G5, and the first ledger line above is A5.

wrong.explanation: G5 sits just above the top line, with no ledger line; the ledger line is one step higher.
C6 is on the second ledger line above (A5 line, B5 space, C6 line).
E5 is inside the staff, in the top space.

items.prompt: In the bass clef, which note sits on the first ledger line below the staff?

answer.explanation: The bottom line is G2, the space below is F2, and the first ledger line below is E2.

wrong.explanation: F2 hangs just below the bottom line with no ledger line; one step lower is the ledger line, E2.
C2 is on the second ledger line below (E2 line, D2 space, C2 line).
C4 is the first ledger line above the bass staff, not below it.

items.prompt: What does a sharp sign do to a note?

answer.explanation: A sharp moves the note to the very next key to the right, one semitone higher.

wrong.text: Raises it by one whole tone
wrong.explanation: A whole tone is two semitones; a sharp raises by only one (a double sharp raises by two).
That is a flat; a sharp raises.
Cancelling is the natural sign's job; a sharp raises the note a semitone from its natural form.

items.prompt: Which key plays F sharp?

answer.text: The black key just to the right of F
answer.explanation: F sharp is one semitone above F, the next key to the right, which is black.

wrong.text: The black key just to the left of F
wrong.explanation: There is no black key between E and F; the key just left of F is E, a semitone below, and sharps raise.
G is a whole tone above F; F sharp is only a semitone up.
E is a semitone below F; sharps move up, not down.

items.prompt: With no key signature, a bar has F sharp on the first beat and later another F on the same line with no sign. What is the second note?

answer.explanation: An accidental applies to later notes on the same staff position until the bar line.

wrong.explanation: Without a new natural sign, the sharp still holds until the bar line.
Accidentals do not add up; the second F is simply F sharp again.

wrong.text: It depends on the hand playing it
wrong.explanation: The rule is about the staff position and the bar, not which hand plays.

items.prompt: With no key signature, F sharp appears in bar 1. In bar 2, an F on the same line has no sign and is not tied. What is it?

answer.explanation: The bar line cancels the accidental; only a tie carries it into the next bar.

wrong.explanation: The sharp held only until the bar line; a new bar starts clean unless the note is tied over.
Nothing lowers the note; once the sharp ends, it is plain F.

wrong.text: F sharp, but only an octave higher
wrong.explanation: Accidentals do not jump octaves; this F is natural, and the sharp never applied to other octaves.

items.prompt: Which key plays F double sharp?

answer.explanation: A double sharp raises a note two semitones: F to F sharp to G.

wrong.explanation: That is one semitone up; a double sharp raises by two.
That is three semitones above F; a double sharp moves only two.
Sharps raise; E is below F.

items.prompt: Which key plays B double flat?

answer.explanation: A double flat lowers a note two semitones: B to B flat to A.

wrong.explanation: That is one semitone down; a double flat lowers by two.
That is three semitones below B; a double flat moves only two.
Flats lower; C is above B.

items.prompt: Which pair of white keys is a semitone apart, with no black key between them?

answer.explanation: E to F (and B to C) are the two white-key pairs with no black key between, so each is a semitone.

wrong.explanation: A black key (C sharp) lies between C and D, so they are a whole tone apart.
F sharp lies between them, so F to G is a whole tone.
B flat lies between them, so A to B is a whole tone.

items.prompt: How many semitones make one whole tone?

answer.explanation: A whole tone is two semitones, as from C to D past C sharp.

wrong.explanation: One semitone is a half step, half of a whole tone.
Three semitones make a minor third, a bigger gap than a tone.
Twelve semitones make an octave.

items.prompt: Which note sounds the same as C sharp on the piano?

answer.explanation: C sharp and D flat are the same black key, two names for one sound.

wrong.explanation: C flat is below C (it is the key B), not above it.
D sharp is the next black key up, a whole tone above C sharp.
B sharp is the key C, a semitone below C sharp.

items.prompt: Which key plays E sharp?

answer.explanation: E to F is a semitone with no black key between, so E raised a semitone is the key F.

wrong.explanation: There is no black key between E and F; one semitone up from E is F.
A sharp always moves the note up a semitone, even when that lands on a white key.
F sharp is two semitones above E; E sharp is only one.

items.prompt: A treble-staff C5 has '8va' written above it. Which C do you play?

answer.explanation: 8va above the notes means play them an octave higher than written: C5 becomes C6.

wrong.explanation: The sign changes the sounding octave; playing as written ignores it.
An octave lower is 8vb, written below the notes; 8va above means higher.
Two octaves higher is 15ma; 8va is one octave.

items.prompt: A bass-staff C3 has '8vb' written below it. Which C do you play?

answer.explanation: 8vb below the notes means play them an octave lower than written: C3 becomes C2.

wrong.explanation: 8vb means lower; the higher octave is 8va.
The sign changes the octave you play; playing as written ignores it.
That is two octaves down (15mb); 8vb is one octave.

items.prompt: Which white key is just to the left of a group of two black keys?

answer.explanation: C sits just below the group of two black keys; D is between them and E just above.

wrong.explanation: D is between the two black keys, not to their left.
F is just left of the group of three black keys.
B is just left of C, at the right end of the group of three.

items.prompt: Which white key is just to the left of a group of three black keys?

answer.explanation: F sits just below the group of three; G and A are between them and B just above.

wrong.explanation: C is left of the group of two black keys.
G is between the first two black keys of the group of three.
E is just right of the group of two, one key before F.

items.prompt: What is the lowest key on a standard 88-key piano?

answer.explanation: The piano runs from A0 at the bottom to C8 at the top.

wrong.explanation: Octave 0 starts at C below the piano's range; the lowest key the piano actually has is A0.
C1 is the lowest C, but A0 and B0 lie below it.
A1 is an octave above the lowest key.

items.prompt: Which note is one white key below middle C (C4)?

answer.explanation: Octave numbers change at C, so the B just below C4 belongs to octave 3.

wrong.explanation: B4 is the B just below C5; octave numbers go up at each C, so the B below C4 is B3.
C3 is seven white keys down, a whole octave.
A3 is two white keys below middle C.

items.prompt: Which note is one octave above A3?

answer.explanation: An octave up keeps the letter and adds one to the octave number.

wrong.explanation: B3 is one white key up, a step, not an octave.
That is the same note; an octave above is a different pitch with the same name.
E4 is a fifth above A3, not an octave.

items.prompt: How many semitones above C4 is the next C?

answer.explanation: An octave spans twelve keys, seven white and five black.

wrong.explanation: Seven is the number of white keys (and letter names) in an octave; with the black keys there are twelve.
Eight counts the white keys from C to C including both ends; in semitones the distance is twelve.
Five is only the black keys in an octave.

items.prompt: In the alto clef, which note is on the middle line?

answer.explanation: The alto clef is a C clef centred on the third line, which makes that line middle C.

wrong.explanation: B4 is the treble clef's middle line; the alto clef puts middle C there.
D3 is the bass clef's middle line.
A3 is the tenor clef's third line; in alto, the middle line is C4.

items.prompt: In the alto clef, which note is on the top line?

answer.explanation: Alto lines from the bottom are F3 A3 C4 E4 G4.

wrong.explanation: F5 is the treble clef's top line; alto sits lower, with middle C in the centre.
A3 is the bass clef's top line, and the alto clef's second line.
E4 is the alto clef's fourth line, just below the top line.

items.prompt: In the tenor clef, which line is middle C?

answer.explanation: The tenor clef is a C clef centred on the fourth line from the bottom.

wrong.explanation: The third line is middle C in the alto clef; tenor moves the C clef up one line.

wrong.text: A ledger line below the staff
wrong.explanation: That is middle C's place in the treble clef.
No common clef puts middle C on the second line; tenor uses the fourth.

items.prompt: In the tenor clef, which note is on the top line?

answer.explanation: Tenor lines from the bottom are D3 F3 A3 C4 E4.

wrong.explanation: G4 is the alto clef's top line; the tenor clef sits a third lower.
F5 is the treble clef's top line.
A3 is the tenor clef's middle line, two lines below the top.

items.prompt: Middle C, written in the alto clef, goes where?

answer.explanation: Alto is a C clef on the third line, so middle C is the middle line.

wrong.text: On one ledger line below the staff
wrong.explanation: That is middle C's place in the treble clef, not the alto.
The alto clef's third space is D4, a step above middle C.

wrong.text: On one ledger line above the staff
wrong.explanation: That is middle C's place in the bass clef.

items.prompt: The bass clef's top-line note, A3, is rewritten in the treble clef at the same pitch. Where does it go?

answer.text: On the second ledger line below the staff
answer.explanation: Below the treble staff: D4 hangs under the bottom line, C4 is the first ledger line, B3 the space under it, and A3 the second ledger line.

wrong.explanation: The top treble line is F5; copying the line's position changes the pitch.
That is A4, an octave higher: the letter matches but the octave does not.

wrong.text: On the first ledger line below the staff
wrong.explanation: That ledger line is middle C, two white keys above A3.

items.prompt: A note moves from a line to the next line up. What is that interval?

answer.explanation: Line to next line passes one space, so it spans three letter names: a third.

wrong.explanation: A step is line to the next space, or space to the next line.
A fourth goes from a line to the second space above it.
A fifth is line to the second line above it.

items.prompt: Counting the way music theory does, what size of interval is C up to E?

answer.explanation: Count both ends: C, D, E is three letter names, so a third.

wrong.explanation: That counts only the gaps between the notes; theory counts every letter name, both ends included.
C to F is a fourth; E is one letter lower.
C to E is four semitones; the size 'third' counts letter names, not keys.

items.prompt: Which C sits in the second space of the bass staff?

answer.explanation: Bass spaces from the bottom are A2 C3 E3 G3, so the second space is C3, an octave below middle C.

wrong.explanation: C4 is middle C, on a ledger line above the bass staff.
C2 is on the second ledger line below the bass staff.
E3 is the third space; the second space is C.

items.prompt: Which landmark note does the treble clef's curl circle?

answer.explanation: The treble clef is a G clef; its curl wraps the second line, G4.

wrong.explanation: That is the bass clef's landmark, marked by its two dots.
Middle C is a landmark, but the treble clef's curl marks G.
E4 is the bottom line; the curl is one line higher, on G.

items.prompt: A note sits above the middle line. Which way does its stem usually go?

answer.text: Down, on the left side of the note
answer.explanation: Notes above the middle line take stems down, drawn from the left side.

wrong.text: Up, on the right side of the note
wrong.explanation: That is for notes below the middle line.

wrong.text: Down, on the right side of the note
wrong.explanation: A down stem hangs from the left side; up stems go on the right.

wrong.text: Up, on the left side of the note
wrong.explanation: Up stems are drawn on the right side, and high notes take down stems anyway.

items.prompt: Which way does the stem of a note on the middle line go?

answer.text: Either way, depending on the notes around it
answer.explanation: Middle-line notes may point either way; the surrounding notes decide.

wrong.explanation: Up is for notes below the middle line; the middle line itself can go either way.
Down is common, but the rule leaves middle-line notes free to match their neighbours.
Every note shorter than a whole note has a stem, wherever it sits.
